value.question: Combine evidence from at least two sources on why single-request transformer inference is memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound.

steps.description: Search the local corpus for technical sources explaining the arithmetic intensity and memory-bandwidth limitations of single-request transformer inference (e.g., why token generation is memory-bound).

Search the web for authoritative sources (papers, blog posts from AI infrastructure teams) that analyze why single-request transformer decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, and fetch primary pages for key claims.
Run a quick calculation comparing FLOPs vs. memory bytes transferred per generated token (arithmetic intensity) for a representative transformer size to demonstrate the bandwidth-bound regime.

key_findings: Modern GPUs have enormous compute power (hundreds of TFLOPs), but they can't get data fast enough to use it; LLM inference is memory-bound, not compute-bound (fetch-7b556b5cc997).
During training, large batches amortize weight loading across many examples, but during inference we often can't batch as much, which is why batching helps only a little (fetch-7b556b5cc997).
For autoregressive decoding, high memory bandwidth is critical for high per-user throughput; serving LLMs requires 100s of GB per server to serve a model instance (fetch-4b5f7bab0259).

For Llama 2 7B on an A10 GPU, the model is memory bound during autoregressive sampling with an arithmetic intensity of 62 ops/byte, which is less than the GPU's 208.3 ops/byte threshold (fetch-f5200c8cbcc1).
gaps: The evidence does not provide a detailed quantitative walkthrough of the roofline model or the exact arithmetic intensity calculation for prefill (context processing) vs decode (autoregressive) phases.

The evidence does not specify which NAS aircraft/spacecraft systems handbook documents (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf) are relevant; those citations appear unrelated to the question about transformer inference memory bandwidth.

value.text: Single-request transformer inference (autoregressive token-by-token decoding) is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound, because each generated token requires streaming the full weight set from HBM to the compute units but performs relatively little arithmetic per byte moved. As the GitHub chapter notes, modern GPUs have enormous compute power (hundreds of TFLOPs) but "can't get data fast enough to use it," making inference memory-bound. The arXiv limit study independently confirms that "high memory bandwidth is critical for high per-user throughput" during autoregressive decodingikuha and that serving requires hundreds of GB per server. During training, large batches amortize weight loading across many examples, but during inference we often cannot batch as much, which is why batching helps only a little. This is a qualified partial answer because neither fetched page provides a full roofline walkthrough; however, both sources support the bandwidth-bound principle for single-request decoding.
